name: Lead Exposure Elimination Project (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result at the defaults by country, each country's births times its branch's discounted years and its own delivery share (regulations 35%, Nigeria at half credit; market switches 65%, Pakistan at its measured 53%, Malawi 90%, the other five 20%).
summary: The Lead Exposure Elimination Project (LEEP) tests paint on sale in low- and middle-income countries and works with governments and manufacturers to take lead out of it; we count its spending from its founding in September 2020 to the end of 2025 against what it won: lead paint rules adopted in seven countries with its support (Nigeria at half credit) and measured switches to lead-free paint in seven more, Pakistan the largest. Each year a market stays free of lead paint spares about a birth cohort the IQ points that paint lead would cost them, valued as later earnings; adults' lead deaths in the same homes are a side effect. At the defaults it comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, but the result is mostly uncertainty: no study measures how much of children's blood lead comes from paint in these countries, and the discount rate and the years a won rule counts move it most, since the benefits come decades later. Every branch is discounted for missing data, and its spices, eyeliner and plastics work has won no change yet, so it counts as cost only.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Share of 2025's spending whose wins come after the end-2025 count
rows.explainer: LEEP tripled its spending in 2025 and started 11 new paint programmes. Its own record puts months to years between the work and a win: Nigeria's rule was signed four months after the LEEP-funded workshop, Liberia's within weeks of LEEP-funded workshops, the Democratic Republic of the Congo's draft five months after its study, Sierra Leone's rule about three years after its study, Zimbabwe's manufacturers' switch two years after theirs, and Malawi's market two years of joint work after its study. LEEP's 2025 spending rose through the year (the Form 990's year to August 2025 implies about $0.36M a month, the calendar year's total about $0.5M a month after it), and its 2026 goals double the regulations from 7 to 14. With a typical lag of about a year, most of 2025's spending buys wins after the count. Our judgment: three quarters (40% to all of it).

rows.label: Nigeria's rule counted as a share of LEEP's other regulations

source.title: LEEP, Nigeria: lead paint regulation and standard
source.quote: NESREA had drafted lead paint regulation in 2020
source.note: SRADev Nigeria had campaigned on lead paint since 2009 with IPEN; LEEP's grant to SRADev (July 2023) paid for the October 2023 workshop, after which the regulation was signed in November and gazetted in March 2024.

rows.explainer: Nigeria has two thirds of the regulation countries' births. LEEP's grant to SRADev Nigeria (July 2023) is LEEP's own resource and in its cost, but much of the work behind the rule came before it and from others' own resources: the regulator NESREA had drafted it in 2020, and SRADev and IPEN had campaigned since 2009. Elsewhere LEEP ran the paint study and worked with the regulator from the start. Our judgment: Nigeria counts at half the credit of LEEP's other rules (20% to 100%), on top of the shared credit share below.

rows.label: Children's average blood lead in low- and middle-income countries (µg/dL)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead), from Ericson et al.'s review of blood lead in low- and middle-income countries.

rows.label: Share of children's blood lead that comes from lead paint
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead): a judgment, as no study measures it in these countries. The country average already takes in that many rural homes are unpainted, so it applies to every child born.

rows.label: IQ points lost per µg/dL of blood lead in childhood
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead), from Lanphear et al.'s pooled analysis of seven cohorts.

rows.label: IQ points a child keeps when lead paint is kept out of the homes
rows.explainer: The blood lead that paint adds, averaged over childhood, times the IQ loss per µg/dL.

rows.label: Increase in earnings per IQ point
rows.explainer: The shared figure (GiveWell, {{row:iq_wage_gain}} per IQ point), read as a gain in ln(consumption).

rows.label: Household sharing multiplier on an earnings gain
rows.explainer: The shared multiplier for later-life income gains shared within the household (facts: givewell_shared).

rows.label: Years an IQ gain raises earnings, discounted
rows.explainer: The shared working life of 40 years (facts: givewell_shared.long_term_benefit_years), discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Average years a year's lead paint keeps exposing children

source.title: Lead Exposure Elimination Project (2021), LEEP cost-effectiveness analysis - Malawi
source.page: p. 2, 'The percentage of homes painted with unregulated paint'
source.quote: The frequency of replacement or repainting of homes is assumed to be 2% per year - in other words, we assume that the average home is repainted or replaced once every fifty years.

rows.explainer: Paint put on walls in one year poisons children for as long as it stays: it flakes and wears into dust, mostly on doors and windows, and repainting covers rather than removes it. LEEP's Malawi analysis assumes a home is repainted or replaced once in fifty years; lead paint on outside walls weathers away sooner and renovation dust removes some. Our judgment: the exposure fades with an average life of 25 years (10 to 50).

rows.label: Years from a child's exposure to working age
rows.explainer: Lead harms the brain most before about age six (exposure centred near age three); earnings start at about 20. Our judgment, 17 years (14 to 20), as EDF's lead-pipe branch of ours takes 15 (10 to 20) for the same chain in older children.

rows.label: Discount for the paint's exposure coming over its life
rows.explainer: The exposure a year's paint would have caused fades at a constant rate over its average life; discounted continuously at the shared rate, its present value is (1/life) ÷ (1/life + ln(1 + rate)) of the undiscounted whole (one birth cohort's worth, below).

rows.label: Discount for the waits until the earnings gain begins
rows.explainer: The paint's exposure over its life, then the wait from a child's exposure to working age, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Birth cohorts' worth of paint exposure averted per year lead paint is kept off the market
rows.explainer: If lead paint has been sold for decades, the paint on walls is many years' sales, and each year's sales cause that year's share of the harm for as long as they last: summed over their life, about one birth cohort's childhood of paint lead. A market growing faster than the population (LEEP's Malawi analysis: about 5% a year) puts more than a year's share in each new year's sales, and paint lost to renovation, replacement or rain puts less. Our judgment, 1 (0.5 to 1.6).

rows.label: Earnings value per child born in a protected country per year of protection, in units of value
rows.formula: iq_points_per_child * iq_wage_gain * resource_sharing * iq_years * income_wait_discount * $uov_per_ln_consumption * cohorts_per_win_year
rows.explainer: The IQ points kept as a gain in ln(consumption) over the working life, shared in the household, after the waits, in units of value, for each birth cohort's worth of exposure averted.

rows.label: Deaths attributed to lead exposure worldwide, 2023

source.title: WHO, Lead poisoning and health, fact sheet (10 June 2026), citing IHME's Global Burden of Disease Study 2023
source.quote: more than 3.5 million deaths globally were attributed to lead exposure in 2023, primarily due to cardiovascular effects

rows.explainer: Lead's deaths from all sources, mostly adults' heart disease from a lifetime's exposure.

rows.label: Births worldwide, 2023

source.title: UN World Population Prospects 2024, births per year (Our World in Data grapher)

rows.explainer: Lead's deaths per year are put against a year's births, so that a birth cohort's worth of paint exposure averted carries a year's worth of paint's share of the deaths.

rows.label: Paint's share of adults' blood lead, relative to its share of children's
rows.explainer: Young children swallow paint dust and flakes by putting their hands and toys in their mouths; adults in the same homes take in much less, and their blood lead comes more from food, work and old exposure stored in bone. Our judgment: paint's share of adults' blood lead is a quarter of its share of children's (10% to 50%).

rows.label: Value of a heart-disease death averted, at the world's ages (units of value)
rows.explainer: The ages of the world's cardiovascular deaths (facts: death_ages) valued by GiveWell's weights by age, the 70-and-over band split by the share at 80 or older, × the value-of-a-life slider: lead's deaths are mostly heart disease in older adults.

rows.label: Side effect: adults' lead deaths averted, value per child born per year of protection (units of value)
rows.formula: lead_deaths_2023 / world_births_2023 * paint_share * adult_vs_child_paint_exposure * lead_cvd_value_per_death * paint_exposure_pv * cohorts_per_win_year
rows.explainer: Lead paint dust also raises the blood lead of the adults in the same homes, which raises blood pressure and heart disease. Lead's deaths per birth, × paint's share of adults' blood lead (its share of children's × the adult ratio), valued at the shared value of a death by age, over the paint's life. The world's deaths over the world's births slightly understate the rate in the protected countries, where blood lead is higher, so this is a little conservative. Illness short of death, kidney disease and children's behaviour problems aren't counted: lead's burden is mostly deaths.

rows.label: Value per child born in a protected country per year of protection, in units of value
rows.explainer: The children's earnings gain and the adults' deaths averted, for each birth cohort's worth of paint exposure kept off the market.

rows.label: Share of the counted wins that happened
rows.explainer: The regulations were adopted and the market switches measured by the end of 2025: a past average counts what was won. How much of each delivers is each branch's implementation row, LEEP's part in it the credit share.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (Your values → How impact is counted; docs/normalization.md 2.9), for regulations and market switches alike. Never the charity's or an evaluator's own years (LEEP's Malawi analysis took 8).

rows.label: Years from a regulation's adoption until it applies
rows.explainer: New limits usually give manufacturers a transition period, and some wait for gazetting before they have legal force: Liberia's rule, passed in January 2025, gives manufacturers three years and had not been gazetted by March 2026 (AllAfrica, 31 March 2026), while Nigeria's was enforceable once gazetted. Our judgment, 1.5 years (0 to 3); delivery after it is the implementation row. The market switches are already happening: no wait.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until a regulation applies
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact of a regulation
rows.explainer: The years a won reform counts, discounted, after the wait until the rule applies.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact of a market switch
rows.explainer: The same years with no wait: the switches are under way.

rows.label: Regulations: value before adjustments (units of value)
rows.explainer: Children protected a year × value per child × the discounted years. Compliance costs: no impact analysis of these rules exists; lead-free pigments were already on sale in Malawi at comparable prices (LEEP's Malawi analysis), so none is counted.

rows.label: Market switches: value before adjustments (units of value)
rows.explainer: The same chain; the switches are voluntary, so no compliance cost is counted (the manufacturers chose them, with free technical help from LEEP).

rows.label: Other lead sources: value before adjustments (units of value)
rows.explainer: Zero until a change is won: studies and pilots by the end of 2025.

rows.label: Expected value of the wins (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The branches summed, for reading; each takes its own delivery share in the outcome.

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, net of where shifted money would have gone, at the mobiliser's share, units of value
rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone. The donors gave it, so the organisation is credited its share of that good (mobiliser_share).

rows.label: Value of the career changes (units of value)
Evidence adjustment: how far the lead-to-IQ-to-earnings chain should be trusted here
rows.explainer: The IQ loss per µg/dL comes from cohort studies that adjust for confounders but can't remove all of them (the slope is backed by the IQ gains after leaded petrol was phased out); the cohorts are from rich countries and Mexico and Yugoslavia, at higher blood lead than today's children in these countries, where the slope is steeper. The IQ-to-earnings link is GiveWell's shared figure, and the paint share has its own row. Our judgment, 0.7 (0.4 to 1.0), a little below the 0.8 of EDF's lead-pipe branch of ours, which rests on EPA's own exposure modelling.

rows.label: Share of the wins that wouldn't have come in the same years anyway
rows.explainer: The years a won reform counts already take in that a rule would come some day anyway (templates.md Convention 5). This row is the part that would have come in the same years regardless: multinational paint companies' own lead-free policies, and the UN Environment Programme's and others' campaign for lead paint laws, which reached some of these markets. Our judgment, 90% (70% to 100%).

rows.label: LEEP's share of the resources behind the wins
rows.explainer: LEEP ran the paint studies, worked with the regulators and manufacturers and paid for workshops and partners' advocacy (its grants are in its cost). Others' resources: the standards bureaus' and ministries' staff time drafting and enforcing the rules, partner NGOs' own work (IPEN members, Pure Earth), the UN Environment Programme's and WHO's alliance, and manufacturers' chemists. Our judgment, half (a quarter to four fifths); the same with credit by share of resources on or off, as the shares are of the work.

rows.label: Share of credit used

rows.label: Regulations: share of the lead paint market made lead-free by the rules, as delivered

source.title: LEEP, 2025 in Review
source.quote: brands representing only 4% of market share are using lead-based raw materials, down from 89%

rows.explainer: A rule on paper removes lead only as far as it is enforced and followed. Five of the seven rules are from 2025 (Liberia's not yet gazetted in March 2026 and with three years for manufacturers to switch), enforcement agreements cover only some of the countries, and Nigeria's market is large and fragmented. LEEP's follow-up testing shows what full delivery can look like: in Malawi, four years after enforcement began, brands using lead-based raw materials fell from 89% of the market to 4% (the paint still over the limit is low-level contamination at two manufacturers), and in Pakistan the oil-based lead paint brands' share fell from 88% to 41% in three years. New rules take years to reach that. Our judgment, 40% of the lead paint removed over the years counted (15% to 70%).

rows.label: Market switches: share of Pakistan's lead paint gone, 2021 to 2024

source.title: LEEP, 2025 in Review
source.quote: market share of brands selling oil-based lead paint for home use has reduced from approximately 88% in 2021 to 41% in 2024

rows.explainer: LEEP's follow-up paint study: the oil-based home-use lead paint brands' share fell from about 88% to 41%, so (88 − 41) ÷ 88 = 53% of the lead paint is gone. The range takes in sampling error and that brands still selling some lead paint may sell less of it.

rows.label: Market switches: share of Malawi's lead paint gone, 2021 to 2025

source.title: LEEP, 2025 in Review
source.quote: brands representing only 4% of market share are using lead-based raw materials, down from 89%

rows.explainer: LEEP's follow-up paint study: brands using lead-based raw materials fell from 89% to 4% of the market (96% gone); two major manufacturers still have low-level contamination over the limit. Our estimate, 90% (75% to 96%).

rows.label: Market switches: share of the lead paint gone in the five countries without a measured share

source.title: LEEP, 2025 in Review
source.quote: more manufacturers reformulated in 2025 in Ghana, Colombia, Senegal, Zimbabwe, Pakistan, Malawi, South Africa and Burundi

rows.explainer: In Zimbabwe manufacturers with over 90% of the market said in 2023 they had started to switch, and in Ghana, Colombia, Senegal and South Africa testing shows more manufacturers switching, but no market share is published. Our judgment: a fifth of the lead paint gone (5% to 50%), below Pakistan's measured 53% because the switches are reported rather than measured and, without a law, some may switch back.
